entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Liu Xin (c. 50 BCE – 23 CE), courtesy name Zijun, was a preeminent Chinese polymath active during the tumultuous transition from the Western Han to the Xin dynasty, a period marked by profound intellectual and political upheaval. As an imperial librarian, astronomer, classicist, mathematician, and politician, Liu Xin stood at the nexus of scholarly endeavor and statecraft, profoundly influencing the transmission and interpretation of classical Chinese texts. His work in establishing a standardized canon for the "Old Text" classics and his contributions to calendrical reform positioned him as a pivotal figure in the intellectual history of early imperial China, shaping the curriculum and philosophical discourse for centuries.

Following in his father Liu Xiang's footsteps, Liu Xin inherited the monumental task of cataloging the imperial library, an endeavor that culminated in the foundational bibliographic work *Qilüe* (七略, "Seven Summaries"), later incorporated into Ban Gu's *Hanshu*. This systematic classification of all known texts laid the groundwork for future Chinese bibliography. Beyond organization, he was a staunch advocate for the "Old Text" versions of the Confucian classics, asserting their authenticity over the "New Text" tradition favored by many Han scholars. His astronomical expertise led to the development of the *Santongli* (三統曆, "Calendar of the Three Systems"), a sophisticated calendrical system adopted by Wang Mang, which accurately predicted celestial phenomena like eclipses and established a new cycle for historical dating.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Liu Xin's contributions to classical scholarship and bibliography profoundly shaped the transmission and interpretation of Chinese texts for over a millennium, and his calendrical reforms influenced subsequent astronomical science. His work established lasting standards for knowledge organization and textual authority.
